title: Online political engagement, cognitive skills and engagement with misinformation: evidence from Sub-Saharan Africa and the United States
screen_reason: Two online panel surveys - Study 1 in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa (N = 901, April-May 2019) and Study 2 in the United States (N = 1,244, February 2020). The aim is a mediation model, but the Study 1 Measures section reports two self-reported sharing shares in parentheses: respondents who have ever shared a political news story online that they later found out was made up (31.1%) and that they thought at the time was made up (23.9%). Those are RECALL (recall_subtype sharing) estimates with a denominator. Everything else - perceived exposure in both studies, and BOTH of Study 2's misinformation-behaviour measures - is reported as scale means only (M = 3.33 and 3.30 for exposure; M = 0.55 and 0.99 for sharing), which the instructions exclude, so no rows come from Study 2 or from the exposure measure.

estimates.platform: Online panel survey (behaviour asked about political news shared online, incl. social media and messaging apps)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have EVER shared a political news story online that they later found out was made up
estimates.denominator: 901 adults (18+) recruited from commercial online panels in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, pooled (country-level breakdowns are not reported)
estimates.definition: Answered yes to: have you ever shared a political news story online that you LATER FOUND OUT was made up (i.e. unwitting sharing of fabricated political news)
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition is given to respondents; the operational wording is a political news story that was 'made up' (fabricated). The companion exposure items use 'not entirely accurate' and 'completely made up'.
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation sharing was measured by asking respondents if they have ever shared a political news story online that a) they later found out was made up? (31.1% shared) and b) they thought at the time was made up? (23.9% shared).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report with no verification; the respondent's own later realisation that the story was made up is the only ground truth. Two-item sharing scale, alpha = .60 (low).
estimates.moderator_quote: The data used in this study was gathered via an online sample fielded between April and May 2019 (N = 901). To recruit participants from Kenya, Nigeria, and South Africa, we employed a public opinion research firm that maintains online panels in these countries. Our sample comprises adults (18 years and above) who were paid financial incentives for their participation. While this data collection strategy in Sub-Saharan Africa tends to overrepresent the urban, young, and more educated sections of the population (Lau et al., 2018), this is also the only segment of the population likely to be exposed to political news content online regularly.
estimates.notes: Value stated verbatim in parentheses. THREE COUNTRIES POOLED: Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa are reported as a single N = 901 figure and cannot be split, so this is a Multi-country row - it must not be assigned to any one nation. Lifetime window ('have you EVER shared'), which makes it non-comparable with past-week/past-month sharing measures. Strong non-representativeness: an incentivised online panel in three countries with limited internet penetration, which the authors acknowledge overrepresents urban, young and educated people (sample mean age 29.6, education 7.92 on a 10-point scale, 57% male); they report that a census-weighted re-analysis followed the same patterns, but no weighted percentage is given. sampling_frame coded survey_sample (a commercial panel with incentives) rather than convenience, though the acknowledged skew makes convenience defensible. topic=politics_elections because both items are restricted to political news stories. This item pairs with the 23.9% row below; the two are NOT mutually exclusive and must never be summed.

estimates.platform: Online panel survey (behaviour asked about political news shared online, incl. social media and messaging apps)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they have EVER shared a political news story online that they thought at the time was made up
estimates.denominator: 901 adults (18+) recruited from commercial online panels in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, pooled
estimates.definition: Answered yes to: have you ever shared a political news story online that you THOUGHT AT THE TIME was made up (i.e. knowing sharing of fabricated political news)
estimates.misinfo_def: No formal definition supplied to respondents; the operational wording is a political news story that was 'made up' (fabricated).
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation sharing was measured by asking respondents if they have ever shared a political news story online that a) they later found out was made up? (31.1% shared) and b) they thought at the time was made up? (23.9% shared).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report with no verification; the respondent's own contemporaneous belief that the story was made up is the criterion. Two-item sharing scale, alpha = .60.
estimates.moderator_quote: Misinformation sharing was measured by asking respondents if they have ever shared a political news story online that a) they later found out was made up? and b) they thought at the time was made up? The two items were summed to create a scale of misinformation sharing (M = .55, SD = .75, alpha = .60).
estimates.notes: Companion item to the 31.1% row: this one captures KNOWING sharing (believed made up at the time), the other UNWITTING sharing (found out later). definition_variant=true marks it as the second, stricter-intent variant of misinformation sharing within the same country x platform cell. The two overlap - the same respondent can answer yes to both - so they cannot be added; the authors summed them only to build a 0-2 index (M = 0.55). A reviewer choosing one representative sharing figure for this study should take the broader 31.1% item. Same pooled three-country denominator and lifetime window caveats as the other row.

missed_or_uncertain: (a) PERCEIVED EXPOSURE yields no row in either study: it was measured on a 4-point frequency scale (how often do you come across political news online that is 'not entirely accurate' and that is 'completely made up') and is reported ONLY as a scale mean - Study 1 M = 3.33, SD = .57, alpha = .62; Study 2 M = 3.30, SD = .95, alpha = .80. No share of respondents above any threshold and no item-level percentages are given anywhere, including Appendices A1 and B1, so nothing is derivable under R8. This is the paper's central exposure construct and it is unusable for prevalence. (b) STUDY 2 (United States, N = 1,244, Qualtrics online quota panel matched to population age and gender, February 2020) yields NO rows at all: its misinformation sharing measure is reported only as M = 0.99, SD = 1.38 on a 0 = never to 2 = more than once scale (alpha = .86), with no percentage for any category. Had the authors reported the share scoring above 0, this would have been a clean US sharing estimate. Worth flagging to an adjudicator: the US sharing mean (0.99) is nearly double the Sub-Saharan African one (0.55) on comparable 0-2 scales, but no share can be recovered. (c) Study 1's own sharing index (M = .55, SD = .75) is likewise a scale mean, not a share. (d) The introduction cites Pew (Silver, 2019) figures that 55% of Kenyan and 69% of South African social media and messaging app users say they frequently or occasionally see articles that seem obviously false or untrue - figures the paper takes from another source, barred by R8. (e) All regression, mediation and moderation results (need for cognition, cognitive ability interactions) are associations, not prevalence.

rob.design: Two cross-sectional online panel surveys. STUDY 1: N = 901 adults (18+) in Kenya, Nigeria and South Africa, fielded April-May 2019 through a public opinion research firm's online panels with financial incentives; the authors explicitly acknowledge the design 'tends to overrepresent the urban, young, and more educated sections of the population', consistent with the realised sample (mean age 29.6, SD 9.95; education 7.92/10; 57% male). No response rate, no per-country Ns, no sampling frame and no weighted estimates reported, although the authors state a census-weighted re-analysis produced the same patterns. STUDY 2: N = 1,244 US adults from a Qualtrics online panel, February 2020, a stratified quota sample matched to population age and gender; again no response rate. All misinformation measures are self-reported with no verification: perceived exposure on a 4-point frequency scale ('not entirely accurate', 'completely made up'; alpha = .62 in Study 1, .80 in Study 2) and sharing from two lifetime yes/no items (alpha = .60 in Study 1, .86 in Study 2). The two-item scales are short and, in Study 1, of low internal consistency. Only Study 1's two sharing items are reported as percentages; every other misinformation quantity in the paper is a scale mean, which is the principal reporting limitation for a prevalence review.
